articles.title: Veja imagens microscópicas vencedoras de prêmio internacional | G1
articles.standfirst: Concurso Nikon Small World recebeu 1.803 fotos de 69 países. Imagem vencedora mostra, em detalhes, gotas saindo de uma impressora a jato de tinta.
articles.summary: Concurso Nikon Small World recebeu 1.803 fotos de 69 países. Imagem vencedora mostra, em detalhes, gotas saindo de uma impressora a jato de tinta.
articles.body:
1º lugar: Gotas de tinta são lançadas por uma impressora sobre o papel em imagem feita com lente de microscópio. — Foto: Ole Bielfeldt/Nikon Small World

Gotas de tinta suspensas no ar, uma aranha coberta de pólen e neurônios dentro do cérebro de um camundongo estão entre as imagens vencedoras de um dos principais concursos de fotografia feita com microscópios .

A edição de 2026 do Nikon Small World recebeu 1.803 imagens de 69 países e premiou 76 registros . O concurso chegou neste ano à sua 52ª edição.

O primeiro lugar ficou com o estudante e fotógrafo experimental alemão Ole Bielfeldt, que registrou gotas de tinta no interior de uma impressora enquanto elas eram lançadas sobre o papel.

Para conseguir a foto, ele adaptou o equipamento e usou uma lente de microscópio.

Em segundo lugar ficou uma imagem de uma aranha-saltadora coberta de pólen, feita por John-Oliver Dum.

O terceiro prêmio foi para Kaelin Wulf e Rachel Flannery, que fotografaram neurônios no cérebro de um camundongo.

Veja abaixo mais imagens do top 20 da edição de 2026:

2º lugar: Aranha-saltadora (Salticus scenicus) aparece coberta de grãos de pólen. — Foto: John-Oliver Dum/Nikon Small World

3º lugar: Neurônios aparecem em imagem ampliada do cérebro de um camundongo. — Foto: Kaelin Wulf e Rachel Flannery/Nikon Small World

4º lugar: Ponta de uma caneta esferográfica vista ao microscópio. — Foto: Justin Theodore Benttinen/Nikon Small World

5º lugar: Interior de uma margarida ainda fechada aparece em detalhes. — Foto: Mike Crutchley/Nikon Small World

6º lugar: Estruturas produtoras de esporos de um fungo mucilaginoso do gênero Hemitrichia. — Foto: Eric Epstein/Nikon Small World

7º lugar: Neurônios humanos produzidos a partir de células da pele crescem em uma pequena câmara de laboratório. — Foto: Bruno Cisterna e Eric Vitriol/Nikon Small World

8º lugar: Grafite de lápis é atingido por uma descarga elétrica de alta tensão. — Foto: Marcel Clemens/Nikon Small World

9º lugar: Célula do revestimento de um vaso sanguíneo do fígado vista ao microscópio. — Foto: Francisco Lázaro-Diéguez/Nikon Small World

10º lugar: Vespa parasitoide emerge da crisálida de uma borboleta. — Foto: Michael Parra Puentes/Nikon Small World

11º lugar: Larva de ouriço-do-mar com 20 dias aparece com os núcleos das células destacados em azul. — Foto: Svenja Carolin Kling/Nikon Small World

12º lugar: Tardígrado troca de pele e deposita um ovo dentro da camada antiga. — Foto: Gonzalo Quiroga Artigas/Nikon Small World

13º lugar: Cristais de estrogênio recristalizado vistos sob luz polarizada. — Foto: Sebastian Sparenga/Nikon Small World

14º lugar: Fungos do gênero Pilobolus crescem sobre fezes de ovelha. — Foto: Mike Crutchley/Nikon Small World

15º lugar: Traqueia de camundongo mostra pequenas estruturas semelhantes a pelos, além de nervos e músculos. — Foto: Julien Resseguier/Nikon Small World

16º lugar: Células da pele de embrião de Xenopus aparecem com diferentes estruturas destacadas por cores. — Foto: Pierre Nouaux, Laurent Kodjabachian e Camille Boutin/Nikon Small World

17º lugar: Tecido intestinal humano cultivado em laboratório mostra as conexões entre as células que formam sua barreira de proteção. — Foto: Gauri Kulkarni/Nikon Small World

18º lugar: Neurônios do hipocampo de um camundongo com 14 dias aparecem com núcleos em verde e proteínas em vermelho. — Foto: Bilal Akhtar/Nikon Small World

19º lugar: Corte do olho de um camundongo mostra vasos sanguíneos da retina e o nervo óptico. — Foto: Satu Paavonsalo e Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World

20º lugar: Concha de abalone, um molusco marinho, vista em detalhes ao microscópio. — Foto: Justin Theodore Benttinen/Nikon Small World

articles.title: Musk pledges $10bn in SpaceX shares for US children: Who really gains?
articles.summary: The pledge, which Trump says will go through tax-friendly ‘Trump accounts’, comes two weeks before the US midterms.
articles.body:
Elon Musk has pledged to give one SpaceX share to every child in the United States next year – a gift that could be worth more than $10bn.

“This will be the first of many,” the world’s richest man wrote on X on Monday.

About 73 million children under 18 live in the US, according to US Census Bureau data.

At Friday’s closing price of $146.03, the pledge would be worth about $10.7bn.

President Donald Trump thanked Musk on his Truth Social platform, and claimed the shares would be given to children “through TRUMP ACCOUNTS”, the tax-friendly investment accounts for children created under his signature tax and spending law last year.

The pledge comes two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections.

Musk is the biggest known donor in the run-up to those elections, having given more than $276m to Republican groups since July.

Musk has not said which children will qualify, when the shares will be handed over, or how.

So how might the giveaway work, and who stands to gain?

SpaceX, the world’s seventh-largest company, began trading on the Nasdaq in June at an initial public offering price of $135 per share. That price has been volatile. SpaceX shares have fallen 35.3 percent since peaking days after the listing.

The shares are currently trading at around $146 a share. Every $1 move in the share price will change the gift’s value by about $73m.

Musk owns 4.8 billion shares in SpaceX outright, according to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in August.

Including unvested awards and stock options, his stake rises to about 6.4 billion shares, or 48.4 percent of the company.

Giving away 73 million shares would reduce his outright holding by about 1.5 percent, barely affecting his control of the company. That’s because his voting power, which is currently about 82 percent because SpaceX has two classes of shares, would fall by only 0.1 percentage points, according to a Bloomberg Opinion calculation.

It would be the largest single gift linked to Trump accounts so far.

Trump said the shares would be held in Trump accounts, and Musk thanked Brad Gerstner, the tech investor behind the accounts, for “helping enable this”.

Nearly 70 million Trump accounts have been opened, one for every child under 18 with a Social Security number, according to the White House. Investments held in Trump accounts can roll up with tax deferred until they are withdrawn when a child turns 18. Alternatively, they can be rolled into a tax-friendly IRA – a retirement account for adults – and continue with the tax-friendly status.

Under Treasury rules published on September 30, donors can now gift individual company stock to children via the accounts. Families and friends making regular contributions to a child’s Trump account are limited to investing low-risk index funds.

Families cannot refuse the shares on behalf of their children and generally cannot sell them for five years, or until the end of the year the child turns 17 if that comes sooner.

Musk cannot sell or trade most of his SpaceX shares until June 2027, the Wall Street Journal reported.

The accounts carry the president’s name, and Trump has tied himself closely to the gift.

He thanked Musk on Truth Social, saying the pledge was “exactly what was envisioned when we created TRUMP ACCOUNTS”.

The White House has presented the accounts as a signature achievement of Trump’s tax law, noting that “every single Democrat voted against” the legislation.

The pledge also marks a public reconciliation. Musk and Trump fell out in 2025 over Trump’s tax-and-spending bill, a rift Trump later called a “little dispute”.

Children will be gaining a share for free, but the gift could also save Musk money.

Donors who give appreciated stock to charity avoid capital gains tax and can usually claim a deduction, the US broadcaster CNBC reported.

As SpaceX’s founder, Musk paid very little for his shares, and selling $10.7bn of them could mean a tax bill of up to about $2.5bn.

It is “a popular practice for particularly high-income taxpayers that would otherwise be paying a high rate”, Will McBride, chief economist at the Tax Foundation, told the broadcaster in May.

Ann Lipton, a law professor at the University of Colorado Boulder, told Inc. magazine that millions of shareholders unable to sell would also have an interest in SpaceX’s success and in “minimising its regulatory burdens”.

For Mitchell Downey, an economist at Stockholm University’s Institute for International Economic Studies who studies political influence in the US, the more striking part of the pledge is what he called “the horseshoe aspect of this” – the idea that right-wing and left-wing policies can curve around and meet.

For decades, progressives have backed the concept of Child Development Accounts, investment accounts for every newborn designed to reduce inequality in wealth, he said. The idea was associated with groups such as the Democracy Collaborative but struggled to gain federal support. Now the idea may become more mainstream as a result of Musk’s gift and Trump accounts.

“It always felt like it might be out of reach,” Downey said. “But I don’t see how Musk’s proposal would be possible without building some infrastructure like this.”

The pledge comes just two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the two houses of Congress. All seats in the House of Representatives and one-third of the Senate are up for re-election.

Trump’s approval rating has meanwhile fallen to a record low of 33 percent, according to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll, with many political observers expecting to see the Republicans lose seats to the Democratic Party as a result.

Musk, who campaigned with Trump in 2024 and spearheaded the president’s Department of Government Efficiency initiative to reduce the size of the federal workforce, has contributed heavily to Republican candidates in advance of the midterm elections.

Is this legal, and why is it controversial?

Downey said he does not believe the pledge raises legal concerns.

“Individuals are allowed to spend their money in support of a politician,” he told Al Jazeera. “The law only gets violated when either it isn’t publicly reported, or it is part of an explicit and documented quid-pro-quo.”

But he said it does raise ethical concerns, though not ones unique to Musk’s approach.

Those concerns relate to “the outsized role that external donors play in US elections”, Downey said. In his view, they apply much like when someone spends heavily on television advertisements for a candidate.

Downey said the precedent was “hard to assess”.

Because Musk is the richest person in modern history, he said, it is perhaps unsurprising that he is “doing something that involves more money than other very rich people have done”.

He pointed to the Gates Foundation’s spending over the past three decades as “a different type of ‘gift to the public’”. The difference, he said, is that the Gates Foundation focuses funding on health crises in countries in Africa and South Asia – not on voters in the US.

Last year, Gates pledged to “give away virtually all my wealth through the Gates Foundation over the next 20 years to the cause of saving and improving lives around the world”.

articles.title: In Southern California, five rival supercolonies of Argentine ants are engaged in a war; researchers reported 15 million worker ants' deaths in a single war
articles.summary: Millions have died when humans went to war against each other ever since the dawn of humanity.
articles.body: Millions have died when humans went to war against each other ever since the dawn of humanity. While animals are known to have their own rivalries and great wars, one among ants, and at such intensity, is a first. In San Diego, a violent war between five rival ant supercolonies has been raging for decades, killing millions upon millions of them annually, as per a report by IFL Science.Argentine ants: All over the worldThe ants in question are Argentine ants, native to South America. The species (Linepithema humile) is highly territorial and prone to aggression towards other insects, using their antennae and chemical signalling to identify whether others are an outside foe or related friend.Throughout the 19th century, the species was accidentally spread across the world through trans-Atlantic shipping. Ants would hitch a ride on some cargo in South America, then find themselves planted across the world, from Europe to Japan. These different parts of the world were seeded by a small number of ants and their population was much less genetically diverse. They all "smelt" the same to each other, and thus nests treated each other as kin.As they stopped fighting and killing each other, many nests with their own queens merged into one huge cooperative "supercolony" spread across vast areas of land. Decades later, the supercolonies found themselves transplanted into yet another corner of the world, creating a battleground when they came into contact with other supercolonies that had strayed down their own path for generations.A war in CaliforniaAccording to a 2006 paper published in the journal Molecular Ecology, southern California is home to five rival supercolonies of Argentine ants. The most dominant colony controls a 1,000-kilometre-long radius of loosely connected nests along the coasts of California, bordered by at least three of the four smaller colonies, each with their own town-sized enclaves.The scientists from UC San Diego explained that the miles-long borders between the territories were sharp, often divided by just a few metres. When the different groups of ants did come into contact, which they appeared to do regularly, violent clashes erupted.Fights between supercolonies were reported in 40% of the site visits by the researchers, averaging around 15,000 deaths per battle. Over months, the scale of death built up to shocking levels. The researchers estimated that at least 15 million worker ants died in a single border skirmish around one of the smaller colonies near Lake Hodges in north San Diego, over their six-month study.No end in sightWhat's remarkable is that the borders barely moved over the months of the research. They might have shifted back and forth from week to week, but neither side was steadily on winning grounds. The supercolonies were stuck in a war that went on forever, losing massive amounts of life but gaining no new territory.What has shocked the researchers is the similarity between this warfare and that among humans. The stalemate has a striking resemblance to the Western Front of the First World War, where the Allied and Central Powers dug into trenches and ground each other down, with the front line barely moving over the course of years. However, unlike the soldiers of World War I, the supercolony stalemate might not have an end.Writing for Scientific American in 2011, biologist Mark W. Moffett explained that Argentine ants are unusual because they don’t show the “dear enemy effect,” in which territorial animals become less aggressive toward familiar neighbouring rivals than toward unfamiliar strangers after long bouts of violence. Through this effect, a kind of demilitarised zone can eventually emerge along the boundaries where violence does not occur. Under the right circumstances, the two territories can break away from each other, and the killing stops.However, Moffett argued that Argentine ants do not have this privilege. In their native South America, the species will often battle it out over floodplains. Rival colonies will often battle, but the fighting will stop each time the waters rise. The conflict never resolves, so they’re programmed to just keep going, and going, and going.

articles.title: They want your blood
articles.summary: In this week’s Optimizer, we look at why health tech companies are partnering with labs to analyze your blood — and what consumers get from that exchange.
articles.body: This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here. It’s an overcast Saturday morning when I give my 12th vial of blood for testing in six weeks. It’s my 24th this year. At this point, I feel like a pro. I schedule these blood draws first thing in the morning so I don’t get hangry, download the requisition papers ahead of time, avoid strenuous exercise for the 24 hours prior, and make sure to drink a glass of water beforehand so my teeny veins are easier for the phlebotomist to find. In fairness, 12 of the 24 vials were ordered by my doctor to monitor ongoing treatment for a few metabolic issues. Eight were to feed my experimental digital twin. The last four are to test an app called Death Clock, which estimates when you’ll die based on your current health. Currently, the app says I’m going to die at 97 years old on Friday, October 5th, 2085. For greatest accuracy, and to calculate my biological age, Death Clock offers a “free” blood panel with its $69 annual subscription. The app also offers various other optional, upsell panels recommended based on the health history you upload during onboarding. It suggested that I add on tests for thyroid function, heart and artery health, and liver function. On top of the blood panels, the app also recommended I try a continuous glucose monitor, buy a smart scale, buy a blood pressure monitor, get a professional VO2 max evaluation, schedule a liver ultrasound, screen for cervical cancer, start taking daily creatine monohydrate, schedule an annual full-body skin cancer exam, get a baseline coronary CT angiography, consider getting APOE testing for Alzheimer’s risk, and get a colonoscopy. I was getting a vampiric promise of longevity. My blood was the roadmap to a long life. If I did everything the app’s “life lab” proposed, I could get an extra 17 years, dying at the ripe old age of 114 on September 12th, 2102. Even so, watching my blood flow into yet another test tube, I thought of my parents. Blood is more than just a mix of plasma, iron, water, and nutrients. Metaphorically, it’s also a history of the family that came before you — and sometimes, though not always, clues to how they died. [Image: You’re all invited to my death day party on October 5th, 2085. Death Clock is a provocative name, but it’s hardly alone in wanting my blood. Oura and Whoop have already added partnerships with Quest Diagnostics, so their users can hand over their blood too. Google recently announced an integration with Function Health, a startup that makes it easy for people to order these kinds of lab tests. When Apple’s new Health app launches, that too will come with a Quest Diagnostics partnership. Blood is in, and more of these partnerships are undoubtedly on the way. It’s not hard to guess why. Blood contains data — the thing that keeps health tech companies fed. In this age of personalized tech, what could be more personal than the stuff literally flowing through your veins? But as with any highly valuable, highly private data source, the user has to get something equally valuable in return. Right now, that seems to be a vague promise to live longer. “The reality is life is precious, life is short, and we’re all going to die. The question is when, and I think culturally, we are in denial about death,” Brent Franson, founder and CEO of Death Clock, tells me. “Our view is we want to shake people and say, ‘Hey, the only thing that matters most in your life is whether or not you exist,’ and you want to take your health seriously so you can exist as long as possible.” Franson says that to help people understand their own health and the changes they need to make, they have to know what’s going on in their bodies — that’s where the blood comes in. It feels like a hyper-literal take on the idea of looking inside oneself to find the answers to life. It’s an alluring premise, but there’s a limit to what any one person can learn from any quantity of blood. Later in our conversation, Franson acknowledged that the greatest predictor of longevity is socioeconomic status. The rich live longer because they can afford better healthcare — and your blood says nothing about what your income bracket will be. Those limits are sobering to witness firsthand. In April 2021, I got a phone call from my cousin in the middle of the night. My mom was struggling to breathe and had been rushed to the hospital. Something had been wrong with her for a while. Her speech had been slurred for a whole month, and she was struggling with phlegm that just wouldn’t go away. My mom insisted it was a stubborn cold. This cousin, a doctor, suspected my mom had a series of mini strokes and was now suffering from a potential combination of both a stroke and heart attack — a cardiocerebral infarction. In the ER, my mom loudly protested that everyone was worried over nothing. Her father had lived to 101. Her mother was alive and doing well at 94. Her blood, our family blood, was destined for a long life, and we had no history of cardiovascular issues. (Never mind that my uncle had nearly died from a stroke the year prior.) She yelled at the top of her lungs that at 72, she was entirely too young to die. The doctors didn’t find what was wrong with her that night. Over the next few months, we ran her through a gauntlet of tests, many of which involved blood draws and machines of all types. It turned out, my cousin was also wrong. My mom didn’t have a mini stroke and her cardiovascular function was perfectly fine. Instead, she died six months later from spontaneous bulbar amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, which has nothing to do with blood. It was in her body that April, but no blood test would’ve found it. ALS wasn’t in our family history — and as genetic testing later revealed, she didn’t carry the gene for it either. There was nothing she could’ve done to prevent it. The other proposition is that running your blood through a health tech app’s algorithm and AI chatbots will tell you more about yourself. It’s presented as a democratizing move that empowers you to take action outside of the 15 minutes you might get with a doctor — or at the very least, helps you to make the most of an appointment. I’ve uploaded my various blood tests to multiple apps, asking their accompanying AI chatbots to analyze my data. The big-picture interpretations are similar. My tests invariably point to an inflamed but improving liver. I had high cholesterol, but medication seems to be working. My cardiovascular labs have begun to look pretty optimal, according to every app. The combination of good fasting glucose and HbA1c alongside improving but mildly elevated fasting insulin suggests I have “managed” insulin resistance. In other words, I have learned that going to the doctor and addressing my myriad metabolic issues is working. I could have told you that without any of this extra data. [Image: A very weird thing to be eating breakfast and then get this notification. I’ve also learned that doctors, health tech features, and AI can look at the same tests and arrive at different conclusions. For instance, absolutely no one agrees about my most recent fasting insulin. I’ve been told it’s everything from normal to borderline high or high. What should I do? Do I need to do anything? I don’t know, because the advice is all over the place. This type of mixed signaling leads to one of two outcomes. You could become a Bryan Johnson type, where you get 15 vials of blood drawn at once and sell your blood-testing protocol as a product. You could obsess over every tiny change. Or you could be like me and find this thinly disguised datamining expedition mainly repackages things you already know. [Image: Most of these daily habits make sense. Most. “Doctors don’t order these 150 biomarker panels like Function Health, and they don’t do it for a good reason. There’s a high false-positive risk in doing that many tests, especially on somebody who’s asymptomatic for most of the tests. It creates a lot of confusion and annoyance, I think, for existing primary care physicians,” says Franson. When I point out that Death Clock also offers an extensive range of blood tests, he says the difference is the app takes a more middle-of-the-road approach. The app only covers a basic panel in the subscription — the rest are à la carte options depending on an individual’s health needs. Same as a doctor would do, he says. Then what’s the point? “What we want to be tomorrow is a full replacement for primary care as it relates to preventive health,” Franson explains, saying that patients should still go to doctors for scenarios like injuries or surgeries. His vision is to provide a sort of telehealth guidance for everyday lifestyle interventions and routine screening procedures. “It’s kind of a Death Clock on the outside, but it’s a Life Lab once you’re in.” The app does offer some solid advice. Get more steps in. Try to stick to a sleep schedule. Limit alcohol. Eat five servings of fruits and vegetables. Do this consistently for the most benefit. There’s some personalized advice. Mine is centered on getting my liver back to normal. But if the “life lab” is mainly telling me to do more of what I’m doing, to focus on lifestyle interventions — if that’s all any of these health apps do, did they really need my blood? If there’s one thing Franson and I agree on, it’s that we’ll all die someday. Everyone and everything you love will die also. That’s objectively scary and painful. “If we were all a lot healthier, didn’t eat processed food, exercised more, focused on sleep, did less drinking and smoking — the average life expectancy would be higher than it is. There’s no debate about that,” says Franson. “We’re more informed than ever; even so, we’re not smarter than we ever were. We just have much more information … but we don’t have a great solution to the uncomfortable fact that we’re all going to die.” I recognized perhaps a bit of my father in what Franson had to say. He liked control and certainty, and insofar as my father could influence death — the ultimate uncertainty — he did. He took daily walks and did light calisthenics well into his 70s. He obsessed over his diet, took endless supplements, and went to the doctor often. He always boasted that he’d live to 100 years old. He didn’t. Though most people would say dying at 88 is a good run, he spent the last 10 years of his life battling Parkinson’s, eventually losing control of his limbs and forfeiting his memories to dementia. More diseases that can’t be found in your blood. Even so, he refused to cede that his end was out of his hands. It led to a lonely, painful, and drawn-out death. Perhaps where we differ is that I’m less afraid of dying. I’m more worried about prolonged sickness, of holding on just to hold on. Counterintuitively, I’m hoping my blood panels don’t extend my Death Clock estimate further into the future. It’s not that I don’t want to live a long life. I’m just uninterested in a long life without good health. I went into this experiment skeptical, but open to the possibility I could learn something. So far, I’ve mostly decided my blood never held the answer to my real question. How do I live a life that allows me to die well?
